exampleAnswers.title: Differentiating a Product Containing a Trigonometric Function

question.explanation:
Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=x^3$ and $v(x)=\cos x .$ So, we apply the product rule:

\begin{align} (x^3 \cos x)' &= u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x) \\[3pt] &= (x^3)'\cdot \cos x + x^3\cdot (\cos x)' \\[3pt] &= \left(3x^2\right)\left(\cos x\right)+\left(x^3\right)\left(-\sin x \right) \\[3pt] &= 3x^2 \cos x - x^3 \sin x \end{align}

example.title: Differentiating a Product Containing a Trigonometric Function

question.explanation:
Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=e^x$ and $v(x)=\tan x .$ So, we apply the product rule:

\[ \eqalign{ (e^x \tan x)' &= u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x)\\ &= (e^x)'\cdot \tan x + e^x\cdot (\tan x)'\\ &= \left(e^x\right)\left(\tan x\right)+\left(e^x\right)\left(\sec^2 x \right)\\ &=e^x\sec^2x + e^x\tan x } \]

exampleAnswers.title: Differentiating a Product Containing an Exponential or Logarithmic Function

question.explanation:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x) = \tan(x)$ and $v(x)=\log(x).$ So, we apply the product rule:

\[ \eqalign{ f'(x) & = \left(\tan(x) \right)' \log(x) + \tan(x) \left(\log(x)\right)'\\[5pt] &=\left(\sec^2(x)\right)\left(\log(x)\right)+\left(\tan (x)\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{x \ln(10)} \right) \\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\sec^2(x) \log(x)} + \dfrac{\tan(x)}{x\ln(10)} } \]

example.title: Differentiating a Product Containing an Exponential or Logarithmic Function

question.explanation:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x) = x^{2}+3$ and $v(x)=\ln(x).$ So, we apply the product rule:

\[ \eqalign{ f'(x) & = \left(x^{2}+3 \right)' \ln(x) + (x^{2}+3) \left(\ln(x)\right)'\\[5pt] &=\left(2x\right)\left(\ln(x)\right)+\left(x^2+3\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{x} \right) \\[5pt] &=2x\ln(x) + \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{x^2+3}{x}} } \]

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Product  at a Given Point

question.text: If a curve $\mathcal C$ is given by $y=(x^3 - 1)e^x,$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=2.$
question.explanation:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=x^3 - 1$ and $v(x)=e^x.$ Then, we have

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=3x^2, \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}=e^x. \]

Applying the product rule gives

\begin{align} \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &= u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}+v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\\[3pt] &=(x^3 - 1) \cdot e^x + e^x \cdot (3x^2)\\[3pt] &=e^x(x^3 + 3x^2 - 1). \end{align}

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=2$ into the formula and get

\begin{align} \left.\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} \right|_{x=2} &=\left.e^x(x^3 + 3x^2 - 1)\right|_{x=2}\\ &=e^{2}(2^3 + 3(2)^2 - 1) \\[3pt] &=19e^{2}. \end{align}

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $19e^{2}.$

example.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Product  at a Given Point

question.text: If a curve $\mathcal C$ is given by $y=(2x+1)\ln{x},$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=1$ is
question.explanation:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=2x+1$ and $v(x)=\ln x.$ Then, we have

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=2, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{x}. \]

Applying the product rule gives

\begin{align} \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &= u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}+v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\\[5pt] &=(2x + 1) \cdot \dfrac{1}{x} + (\ln{x}) \cdot 2\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2x + 1}{x} + 2\ln{x}. \end{align}

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=1$ into the formula and get

\begin{align} \left.\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} \right|_{x=1} &=\left.\left(\dfrac{2x + 1}{x} + 2\ln{x}\right)\right|_{x=1}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2(1) + 1}{1} + 2\ln{1} \\[5pt] &=3. \end{align}

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{3}.$
